title: 1914 French mobilization
text:
thumb|"General mobilization order" poster dated August 2, 1914, held by the French National Archives.
thumb|Édouard Detaille, Le Rêve (The dream), 1888: painting showing Third Republic conscripts on maneuvers, dreaming of their predecessors. This patriotic painting, measuring three by four meters and winning a prize at the [REDACTED] Salon, was purchased by the French government and reproduced in large numbers.
thumb|Soldiers of the 66th Infantry Regiment march with flags at the end of their rifles towards the station in Tours on the morning of August 5, 1914, arriving at Flavigny-sur-Moselle (near Nancy) on August 6.

The [REDACTED] French mobilization was the set of operations at the very start of World War I that put the French Army and Navy in a position for war, including the theoretical call to arms of all Frenchmen fit for military service. Planned long before 1914 (via Plan XVII), each man's assignment was based on his age and residence.

It was triggered in response to equivalent measures taken by Germany, the French mobilization took place over [REDACTED], from August 2 to 18, 1914, and involved transporting, clothing, equipping and arming more than three million men in all French territories, both in metropolitan France and in some of the colonies, and then transporting them by rail to the potential theater of war, which at the time was considered to be the Franco-German border.

Such event had political (Sacred Union), socio-economic (due to the departure of almost all young men) and, of course, military consequences (the start of the Battle of the Frontiers). It was the first time that a general mobilization was declared in France (in 1870, only the professional army was mobilized); the second took place in 1939. In [REDACTED], [REDACTED] men were mobilized; in total, throughout the war, some 8,410,000 French soldiers and sailors were mobilized, including 7% indigenous soldiers.

 Preparation 
The Industrial Revolution transformed the art of warfare, not only through the development of weapons and equipment, but above all through the ability of states to effectively mobilize armies with million of men. Since it was economically and socially impossible to keep them all permanently in uniform, they were left to live civilian lives during peacetime, and states mobilized them in the event of conflict, hoping to keep it short.
alt=An entrance gate between two gatehouses, opening onto a vast courtyard, the latter enclosed in the background by a [REDACTED]-storey building.|thumb|Most French towns served as garrisons: here, the entrance to the Colbert barracks in Reims in [REDACTED] (home to the 132nd infantry regiment).
From the end of the 19th to [REDACTED], the [REDACTED] army was a conscription army, like all the armies of the great European continental powers of the time: A small cadre of volunteer career officers and NCOs would be supplemented by millions of reservists, who had received training through their mandatory two-year-service at age 20 and periodic refresher trainings.
Only a small proportion of its units were fully composed of professional soldiers (notably some of the colonial troops and the Foreign Legion).

This was in line with the egalitarian ideology of some Republicans under the Third Republic, in a more militaristic and patriotic context: after 1871, conscript societies (whose members practiced gymnastics, shooting and military instruction from adolescence) multiplied, the Ministry of National Education set up a military education commission in 1881, the League of Patriots was founded in 1882, and schools formed school battalions as part of citizenship education, marching in uniform on July 14th and carrying "school rifles" from 1882 to 1889. By 1913, 221 provincial towns had garrisons, making uniforms a common sight on the streets, with parades, retreats (evening marches through the streets), military music and more.

 Legislation 
alt=Company firing a salvo in line.|thumb|French infantry unit on maneuvers, 1889. Each capable man is trained during his service, then later returns to uniform for training "periods".
Following the Franco-Prussian War of 1870, the Third Republic organized the recruitment for its armies with the law of July 27, 1872 (or the Cissey law): "" ("any Frenchman may be called up, from the age of twenty to that of forty"),Army Recruitment Act of July 27, 1872, published in the Journal Officiel of August 17, 1872.  (In French). service was for five years, with selection by lottery, but with the possibility of being discharged (short stature, deformity, respiratory illness, etc.), replaced or exempted (family responsibilities, clergymen, teachers, etc.). Service was reduced from five to three years by the law of July 15, 1889 (or the Freycinet law).Army Recruitment Act of July 15, 1889, published in [REDACTED] of July 17, 1889.  (In [REDACTED]). This situation was reformed by the law of March 21, 1905 (or the Berteaux law),The 1905 law on universal service is explained partly by the warmongering and [REDACTED] climate that culminated in the Tangier crisis that same year, but also by the domestic policies of the Rouvier government (which was predominantly radical) with the law on the separation of Church and State that same year. which abolished the drawing of lots, replacements and exemptions: henceforth, all men could be called up for two years.Law of March 21, 1905 amending the law of July 15, 1889 on Army recruitment and reducing to two years the length of service in the active Army, promulgated in the Journal Officiel of March 23, 1905,  (In French). Finally, the law of [REDACTED] (or the Barthou law) increased military service from two to three years.Law of August 7, 1913, amending the laws concerning the infantry, cavalry, artillery and engineers, with regard to the size of units and setting the conditions for recruitment into the active army and the duration of service in the active army and its reserves, promulgated in the Journal officiel of August 8, 1913,  (In French).

The theoretical consequence of these laws was that, between 1905 and 1914, every French male who reached the age of 20 (just before the age of majority at the time) had to be registered on a nomination list, then do his military service for two, then three years in the active army (from age 21 to 23), before being returned to civilian life. For the eleven years following his service, men were assigned to the military reserve force (from age 24 to 34), then to the Territorial Army for [REDACTED] (from age 35 to 41), and finally to [REDACTED] for another seven years (from age 42 to 48). Men doing their service were transferred to active regiments, theoretically recruited locally; after their service, they were called up three times for maneuvers and exercises, two times for reservists (each one for four weeks) and one time for territorial army reservists (of [REDACTED]). In theory, men declared unfit for service due to physical incapacity were still subject to military obligations, in the form of auxiliary service (in offices, depots, the health service, etc.). A final case is that of the "special assigned", i.e. customs officers, forest hunters, men in field railway sections, and post and telegraph officers.
alt=Painting showing officers checking conscripts' rooms.|thumb|Édouard Detaille, Inspection des chambres (Room Inspection), 1885.Each year, a "class" of conscripts was recruited: a class is a group of men born in the same year and fit for service. The number of a class corresponds to the year of its census, generally taken in [REDACTED] in which they turned [REDACTED]; conscription took place the year after the census, in autumn. When mobilized, men from the active forces and the youngest reservists formed the units sent into combat, while older reservists were destined to form reserve regiments kept behind the front or to fill depots while waiting to replace casualties. The men of the territorial army formed units for tasks behind the front, such as the garrisoning of squares or entrenchment work. Finally, men from the Territorial Army Reserve were to be used to guard railroads and the coast.

The French Navy recruited its personnel in a different way, based on maritime recruitment: men engaged in maritime or river navigation were required to serve in the "army of the sea",Regulation of November 7, 1866 and law of December 24, 1896 on maritime registration, published in the Journal officiel of December 27, 1896,  (In French). with a [REDACTED] term of service in peacetime. However, as the fleet needed a large number of qualified technicians, recruitment was nationwide, with maritime enrollment providing only half of the fleet's manpower in the event of mobilization.

 Planning 
alt=The general in simple uniform, the civilian in jacket and bowler hat, both wearing binoculars and boots.|thumb|The two main leaders of the French armed forces in 1914: on the left, Joseph Joffre ( Commander-in-chief of the Army); on the right, Adolphe Messimy (Minister of War).
The entire mobilization was planned by the General Staff of the Army, headed since 1911 by Major General Joffre, in particular its [REDACTED] (organization and mobilization of the army, headed in 1914 by Lieutenant colonel Émile Giraud) and [REDACTED] bureau (stages, railroads, troop transport by rail and water, headed by Lieutenant-Colonel Camille Ragueneau).

The plan applied in 1914 was Plan XVII, prepared in 1913 by the General Staff and validated by the Superior War Council. It provided for the mobilization of men, their concentration on the borders, their organization into several armies and the direction of the first offensives. But as all this would take around a fortnight, some of the active troops also needed to cover this mobilization. The role entrusted to the navy, which was outclassed by the German navy, was simply to protect troop convoys from Algeria and Morocco (in the hope that Italy would be neutral) and to block the English Channel to [REDACTED] ships (in the hope of British support).

 Troops organization 
In the event of partial mobilization (motivated by the "threat of aggression characterized by the gathering of armed foreign forces"), only the two youngest reserve units were called up. In the event of general mobilization, everyone was called up, without any individual notification. In his military brochure, each man was given a route sheet ("fascicule de mobilisation", or mobilization booklet, model A was pink if he needed to use the railroads, model A1 was light green if he had to march ) with his call-up date and route (free of charge) to his base, where he was dressed, equipped and armed.
alt=Infantry company souvenir photo.|thumb|The 12th company of the 1st infantry regiment in [REDACTED], stationed in Cambrai. Units were generally recruited locally, particularly in the infantry: soldiers of the 1er RI mainly come from the Cambrai district.

The different types of unit, theoretically recruited locally, were housed in the same barracks:

 Men doing their military service formed the backbone of the active regiments, mainly the 173 infantry regiments (numbered from 1 to 173), plus the 59 colonial and indigenous infantry regiments, the 89 cavalry regiments, the [REDACTED] artillery regiments, the 11 engineer regiments, as well as the service units (crew, management, health, aeronautics corps, etc.)
 On Day 2, the arrival at the depots of the three youngest classes of reservists must bring all active regiments up to full wartime strength
 They were then replaced by the remaining reservists, who were to form reserve infantry regiments created during mobilization (numbered [REDACTED] to [REDACTED]) in infantry regiment depots (numbered by adding [REDACTED] to the number);
 Finally, the territorial infantry, who formed [REDACTED] territorial infantry regiments, at least one in each military district subdivision.

Each infantry depot completes an active regiment (with three battalions), increasing it from 2,000 men to just over 3,200, then sets up a reserve regiment (with two battalions, numbered [REDACTED] and 6), followed by a territorial regiment. Finally the guard posts for communication routes (railroads, canals, telephone and telegraph lines). Each cavalry depot reinforces its cavalry regiment with [REDACTED] reserve squadrons; each artillery depot completes its artillery regiment and creates a reserve group (composed of several batteries); each engineer depot reinforces its regiment with new companies. A few hundred reservists are maintained in each depot to replace future losses.

The vote by the Chamber of Deputies on the Law of Three Years in 1913 was requested by the Army Staff, which wanted to have as many active units as its German counterpart, the Deutsches Heer (for fear of a possible sudden attack). Thanks to this law, the peacetime army grew from 520,000 to 736,000 men in uniform, each company from 90 to 140 men, with ten new infantry regiments (nos. [REDACTED]). This force was structured into 22 corps, each assigned to a military region (or "corps region": in 1914 there were twenty in Metropolitan France, plus one in Algeria).

Between 1914 and 1918, the core tactical element was the infantry division. On August 2, 1914, France mobilized 93 divisions, including 45 active, 25 reserve, 11 territorial, 2 colonial and 10 cavalry divisions. By November 11, 1918, France had 119 infantry divisions.

In 1914 the infantry division comprised:
 [REDACTED] infantry regiments with 3 battalions
 1 field artillery regiment with [REDACTED] groups
 1 cavalry squadron
 1 engineer company

 3 infantry regiments with 3 battalions
 1 field artillery regiment with 3 groups
 1 heavy artillery group
 1 cavalry squadron
 1 engineer company
 1 squadron

 Transportation to the border 
alt=Northern part of France, crossed by several concentric lines all leading to the Franco-German border.|thumb|Diagram showing the various lines used to transport army corps.
Mobilization was determined by rail resources and by the strategy planned for the start of the conflict. The transport of all troops, known as "concentration", mobilized the majority of rolling stock, requisitioned on the advice of the Minister of War:Decree of February 5, 1889 organizing military service on the railroads and decree of December 8, 1913 regulating strategic transport by rail,  one train was needed for a battalion, [REDACTED] trains for an infantry regiment, four for a cavalry regiment, seven for an infantry brigade, 26 for an infantry division and [REDACTED] for an army corps.  These trains were made up of 34 (for a squadron) to 47 (for a battalion) wagons, making for 400-meter-long convoys, with passenger carriages, goods wagons (at a rate of eight horses or forty men per wagon)After the First World War, the OCEM (Office central d'études de matériel de chemins de fer, or Central Office for Railway Material Design) standardized the wagons with the words "Hommes 40 - Chevaux en long 8" (Men 40 - Horses in length 8) on them. and flat wagons (for vans and cannons), as required.

As a result, railroads were extensively developed for military reasons, each subprefecture was connected (Freycinet plan from 1879 to 1914), double tracks led eastwards (notably those from Paris to Nancy and [REDACTED] to Belfort) with ring roads between them, while some stations were enlarged (e.g. Gare de Paris-Est). Ten lines crossing metropolitan France were prepared by [REDACTED] on the execution of the concentration (l'instruction générale sur l'exécution de la concentration) of February 15, 1909, rectified on April 4, 1914, each line designed to transport [REDACTED] army corps from their military regions to landing stations behind the concentration zone. From [REDACTED] of mobilization, these lines were to carry the second stage of the covering corps (the army corps stationed near the German border); on the 3rd and 4th days, the cavalry; from the 4th to the 10th day, all the army corps, starting with the "hasty" divisions of the 2nd, 5th and 8th corps (from the 4th to the 6th day); for day 13, all reserve divisions must be deployed; on day 16, the Army of Africa (part of the 19th Army Corps) arrived; finally, for [REDACTED], all territorial divisions, fleets and logistics must be in place.

Overseas troops were a special case: the 19th Army Corps (mainly recruited and stationed in Algeria) had to supply [REDACTED] divisions (the 37th and 38th), which had to cross the Mediterranean on requisitioned ships and under the protection of French squadrons to land at Sète and Marseille. Colonial troops in the colonies were not included in the mobilization and concentration plan.
+Railway lines for troop concentration. This list of lines and stations has been refined on the basis of the marching and operations diaries of the major units, see document:  Line A concerned the 14th Army Corps, departing from Lyon station, then crossing Bourg-en-Bresse and [REDACTED] to disembark at stations around Lure and Épinal.
 Line B involved the 8th and 13th Army Corps, departing from the Clermont-Ferrand, Saint-Étienne, Bourges, and Dijon stations and converging at Charmes.
 Line C involved the 15th and 16th Army Corps, departing from Marseille and Montpellier stations, then heading up the right bank of the [REDACTED], passing through Mâcon, [REDACTED], Langres and Mirecourt, ending at Pont-Saint-Vincent.
 Line D involved the 9th and 18th Army Corps, departing from stations in [REDACTED], [REDACTED], [REDACTED], and Châteauroux, passing through Tours, Orléans, Troyes, Chaumont and Neufchâteau to arrive around Toul and Nancy.
 Line E covers the 12th and 17th [REDACTED], with stations in Toulouse, [REDACTED], Périgueux and Angoulême, passing through [REDACTED] and Brienne-le-Château to end at Commercy. Line F concerned [REDACTED], departing from the Orléans, [REDACTED], and Paris-Est stations and disembarking near Bar-le-Duc and Saint-Mihiel.
 Line G concerned the 4th and 11th Army Corps, departing from Vannes, Nantes, and Le Mans stations, then passing through Versailles, Choisy-le-Roi, and Reims, before ending around Verdun.
 Line H is for the 3rd and 10th [REDACTED], departing from Rennes and Rouen stations, via [REDACTED], Soissons, and Rethel, to land near Vouziers.
 Line I concerned the 2nd Army Corps, departing from Amiens station, via Laon, Mézières, and Sedan, finishing around Stenay and Dun.
 Line K concerned the 1st Army Corps, departing from Lille station, then via Douai, Valenciennes, and Avesnes, disembarking around Hirson and Rimogne.

 Precautionary measures 
Troops were stationed directly along the Franco-German border to protect mobilization from the very first day, relying on fortifications in the East. In the event of diplomatic tension, The instruction for preparing for mobilization (l'instruction sur la préparation de la mobilisation) provided for six groups of measures to be taken successively:

 group A (precautionary measures), recall of officers, volunteers and troops on the move;
 group B (surveillance measures), surveillance of the border and telegraph and telephone offices;
 group C (protective measures), guarding fortified structures and engineering works;
 group D, coastal surveillance and protection;
 group E (preparatory organizational measures), call-up for exercise of gendarmes, certain reservists and territorial guards of border communication routes, as well as the location of necessary horses;
 group F (preparatory measures for operations), loading of mine devices (to destroy border engineering structures), firing on suspicious aircraft, mobilization exercises for border garrisons, interruption of international power lines.Instruction on the preparation of mobilization of February 15, 1909, updated on April 4, 1914, appendix 2, cited in 
The "cover" (protection) of the mobilization was provided by five army corps, the first echelon of which was almost fully manned in peacetime, prepositioned along the Franco-German border: part of the 2nd corps at Mézières, the 6th corps at Verdun and Saint-Mihiel, the 20th corps at Toul and [REDACTED], the 21st corps at Épinal and Saint-Dié and the 7th corps at Remiremont and Belfort. Their mission under the XVII plan was "initially, to stop enemy reconnaissance or detachments seeking to penetrate the territory, and subsequently, to delay the march of larger corps that could disrupt the landing and concentration of armies". These corps were theoretically available in two echelons: the first between the 3rd and 8th hour of mobilization, the second from the 2nd to the 4th day; the 12th Reims division was to serve as reserve. Between days 4 and 6, the cover was to be reinforced by three "hasty" divisions (cover reinforcements) provided by [REDACTED] (the [REDACTED] division), the 5th corps (the 9th Orléans division, temporarily transferred to the 6th corps) and the 8th corps (the 15th Dijon division, loaned to the 21st corps).

 Outbreak 
Relations between Germany and France at the start of the 20th century were marked by a series of diplomatic tensions, most notably the two Moroccan crises: the Tangier crisis of 1905 and the Agadir crisis of 1911. However, it was through the alliances that these two states were forced to declare their mobilization.

 July Crisis 

The casus belli of the Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinandt triggered a succession of ultimatums, mobilizations and declarations of war that quickly spread to Germany and then France. On July 25, 1914, the Kingdom of Serbia decreed its mobilization in response to the Austro-Hungarian ultimatum; on the same day, Austria-Hungary announced partial mobilization from the 28th. On the 29th, the Russian Empire followed with a partial mobilization due to start on July 30. On [REDACTED], the Tsar ordered general mobilization, which had no other consequences than the inevitable Austrian (from [REDACTED]) and German mobilizations. In France, at [REDACTED] on July 30, Chief of Staff Joffre asked War Minister Messimy for an order to mobilize, or at least to cover the borders, but did not receive it. The General warned the Minister: "If what we know of German intentions proves true, the enemy will enter our territory without firing a shot."
alt=Baron's standing portrait|thumb|Baron von Schoen, [REDACTED] ambassador to France.
On the 31st, the German Empire decreed Kriegsgefahrzustand (a state of war danger: requisitions, border closures, etc.): Joffre again called for mobilization: "It is absolutely necessary that the government should know that, from [REDACTED] onwards, any delay of twenty-four hours in calling up reservists and sending the covering telegram will result in a retreat of our concentration force, i.e. in the initial abandonment of part of our territory" He obtained the covering order, but not the mobilization order: he sent the order by telegram at 5:40 p.m. to the various units, with application from 9 p.m. At 7 p.m., the German ambassador to France, Schoen, met the President of the Council, Viviani, and under the orders of the German Chancellor asked him whether France would remain neutral in the event of [REDACTED] war: the Frenchman procrastinated ("allow me time to think").

 Mobilization order 
At 11 a.m. on August 1, Schoen met Viviani again to obtain the reply that "France will be guided by its interests". At 3:45 p.m., the French governmentViviani did not sign the order, which was signed only by the Ministers of War and the Navy. decreed the start of general mobilization on August 2. By 5:00 p.m. Kaiser Wilhelm II ordered the German mobilization, then declared war on Russia at 7 p.m. On the evening of the 2nd, Germany told the Belgian government not to oppose the passage of German troops through Belgium. On the 3rd, the German ambassador transmitted the declaration of war to France to the head of the French government at 6:45 p.m. (on the basis that French aircraft had attacked German territory) and left Paris, while Belgium refused to let German troops through.

The mobilization order was issued by the "Decree ordering the mobilization of the Army and Navy on August 1, 1914", published in the Journal Officiel on August 2. The telegram giving the mobilization order was sent from Paris at 3:55 p.m. on August 1 to corps, division and regiment commanders, as well as to prefects, who relayed it to sub-prefects and mayors; isolated rural communes were informed by gendarmes (on horseback or by car), then to hamlets by messengers sent by the mayors. (notes taken by village teachers in Isère, Drôme and Hautes-Alpes). The first poster was put up on [REDACTED] at 4pm on the corner of [REDACTED] and Rue Royale. The entire population was informed on [REDACTED] by posters, printed since 1904 (Army Museum, educational brochure) (only the date needed to be completed), posted on public roads in each communeLaw of March 19, 1875 on Mobilization by means of posters and publicity, published in the Journal officiel of March 26, 1875,  and then by the tocsin sounded by church and belfry bells.

 First reactions 

 Astonishment then enthusiasm 
The announcement of mobilization did not trigger widespread enthusiasm: as historian Jean-Jacques Becker points out, "probably the most widespread feeling among all sections of the population was one of surprise", particularly in rural areas where the press was less widely distributed than in cities. The astonishment expressed at the time clearly indicates that the mobilization initially took the population by surprise, as in Charente village Aignes:

Similarly, in [REDACTED], a town in the Drôme region, a schoolteacher testifies: "The population, although prepared for the war for several days by the press, learned the unfortunate news with a sort of stupor. I saw some women crying. The men looked sad, but determined."Testimony of M. Roux, schoolteacher in Nyons, quoted in  

Analyzed by Jean-Jacques Becker, these documents show the different stages of popular reaction. The initial astonishment was often followed by a certain despondency: "consternation, sadness and anguish were widespread, far more so than feelings dictated by the patriotic impulse", and expressions of enthusiasm were rare. President Raymond Poincaré's proclamation, posted and published in the newspapers on August 2, was reassuring, emphasizing "mobilization is not war; on the contrary, in the present circumstances, it appears to be the best means of ensuring peace with honor. The government, strengthened by its ardent desire to reach a peaceful solution to the crisis and shielded by these necessary precautions, will continue its diplomatic efforts and still hopes to succeed. It is counting on the composure of the noble nation not to give way to unjustified emotion; it is counting on the patriotism of all Frenchmen, and knows that there is not one who is not ready to do his duty. At this hour, there are no more parties, there is an eternal, peaceful and resolute France. There is the entire country of law and justice, united in calm, vigilance and dignity".

However, the mood had changed by the time the soldiers left for their barracks, as described above in Aignes. Whereas before, expressions of enthusiasm had been infrequent, now they were more spectacular, particularly at the embarkation stations for mobilized soldiers, demonstrating a genuine patriotic impulse imbued with seriousness and a determination to do one's duty, despite the frequent tears shed by the women or the more or less heart-rending farewells. How can this change in mood be explained? According to Jean-Jacques Becker, revanchist sentiments linked to the 1870 war and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine played little part. French public opinion was dominated by the idea of a peaceful France, obliged to defend itself against outright German aggression. Under these conditions, refusing to fight was out of the question. Men set off, "not with the enthusiasm of a conqueror, but with the resolution of a duty to be fulfilled", an idea also reflected in the testimony of historian Marc Bloch, who was himself mobilized: "Most of the men were not cheerful: they were resolute, which was better."

This commitment, which was measured if resolute, was not incompatible with displays of patriotic enthusiasm in the streets, whether in the form of parades, crowds or military songs; nor did it prevent nationalist and xenophobic outbursts, notably the looting of stores with Germanic names (on the night of August 2 to 3, [REDACTED], and again the following day, the Maggi dairy stores, although Swiss-branded, were looted. The same company's laboratory was set on fire; the Pschorr tavern on boulevard de Strasbourg, the Appenrodt food store on rue des Italiens, the Muller brasserie on rue Thorel and the Klein boutique on boulevard des Italiens were ransacked); the black veil was removed from the Strasbourg statue on place de la Concorde, etc.). This catharsis continued in [REDACTED] that followed, with, for example, the renaming of rue de Berlin to rue de Liège on August 15 (in tribute to the Belgian defenders of the siege of Liège), avenue d'Allemagne to avenue Jean-Jaurès on August 19 (following a petition from the avenue's residents) and the homonym metro stations (Liège and Jaurès), the café viennois was renamed the café liégeois, berlingots became "parigots", German shepherds became Belgian shepherds and [REDACTED] became "eau de Pologne".

However, these collective manifestations of intense patriotic or even nationalist fervor were very much in the minority, confined to a few towns: as Stéphane Audoin-Rouzeau and Annette Becker point out, the motivation of rural populations (the majority in France) was clearly distinct from, but not contradictory to, a certain urban enthusiasm, "the leading edge of a general consent centered on resignation and acceptance - sometimes overwhelm - and then the growing resolution of the majority".

 Sacred union 
Military and political leaders were worried about the possible refusal to obey by civilians called up as reservists: they feared that the number of insoumis (deserters) would be significant, and that pacifist demonstrations would take place. Several opposition unions and political parties, notably the CGT and SFIO, had taken anti-militarist stances before the crisis broke out, and were planning a general strike (the refusal to obey mobilization orders) to prevent the outbreak of conflict. On [REDACTED] and [REDACTED], SFIO leader Jean Jaurès was in Brussels for a meeting of the bureau of the Second International and a meeting with German socialist leaders, with the aim of coordinating their pacifist actions. Faced with these expected difficulties, the French Ministry of the Interior had planned for the systematic arrest of anti-militarist leaders in the event of mobilization: the Carnet B was to provide a list of 2,500 individuals "whose attitude and actions may be likely to disturb order and hinder the smooth running of mobilization services".).

However, the surge of patriotism and the assassination of Jaurès in Paris on July 31 led [REDACTED] to rally to the "Sacred Union" called for by President Poincaré in his speech on August 4. The CGT announced that it was putting its Paris premises on [REDACTED] at the disposal of the Army Medical Corps. [REDACTED], General Secretary of the CGT, proclaimed at Jaurès's funeral: "In the name of the trade unions, in the name of all those workers who have already joined their regiments, and in the name of those, including myself, who will be leaving tomorrow, I declare that we are going to the battlefield with the determination to repel the aggressor." As a result of these reactions, Interior Minister Louis Malvy instructed prefects not to use Carnet B, even though a few arrests were made in the Nord and Pas-de-Calais regions. The SFIO voted for the war loans, then joined the government in the reshuffle of August 26, gaining the Ministries of War and Foreign Affairs.

 Proceedings 
The mobilization of 1914 was divided into three periods: the covering period (August 2 to 7), during which reservists were called up under the protection of covering troops; the concentration period (August 8 to 13), during which active and reserve troops were moved to the frontier; and the start of the period of major operations (August 14 to 18), during which territorial troops, fleets, and logistics were put in place.

 Reservists recalled 
Not all men were mobilized at the same time, but gradually, depending on their status. The mandatory date of arrival at the depot (indicated in days after the first day of mobilization) appeared on the mobilization booklet (a double sheet) attached by staples to the back cover of the military record booklet,  which each man had to keep for his 28 years of military service (three years in the active service, eleven in the reserve, seven in the territorial service and seven in the territorial reserve), including during his travels, and even if he lived abroad.

The 200,000 men of the Territorial Reserve assigned to guarding transport routes were mobilized on the eve of the first day of mobilization (i.e. [REDACTED]), to protect important railroads and engineering structures close to their homes (usually less than ten kilometers away, or 6.2 miles).

In two weeks, the French army went from 686 to 1,636 infantry battalions, from [REDACTED] to 596 cavalry squadrons, from 855 to 1,527 artillery batteries and from 191 to 528 engineer units. Its structure grew from 54 divisions in metropolitan France (including ten cavalry divisions, not counting units in the French North Africa) in peacetime to 94 divisions (46 active, 25 reserve, 13 territorial and 10 cavalry) standing on the ready. In addition, there were 21 army squadrons (each with eight aircraft), two cavalry squadrons, five airships, four companies of local balloonists, and 212 sections of the automotive service (transporting troops, equipment, medical supplies and fresh meat). Departure for the border was on schedule, with the unit theoretically fully manned and equipped.

 Concentration 

 Transportation problems 
alt=Wagons full of soldiers pull away from the station platform.|thumb|Departure of a train of mobilized soldiers from Gare de Paris-Est, August 2, 1914.
The concentration of almost the entire French army corps (minus the 680,000 men still in depots, the 210,000 men guarding the communication routes, the 821,400 men assigned to strongholds,Tableau des effectifs mobilisés (Table of mobilized staff),  the [REDACTED] men at sea and the units deployed in the colonies) near the Franco-German border was carried out in 1914 by rail. This huge move, organized by the General Staff, was made possible by the requisitioning of the railroads (Nord, Est, PO, PLM and [REDACTED]), which lost all autonomy (except financial) on the evening of July 31.Télégramme du ministre de la Guerre à celui des Travaux publics, à 18 h [REDACTED] (Telegram from the Minister of War to the Minister of Public Works, [REDACTED] on July 31, 1914), cited in  This requisition was total: personnel, installations and all equipment were under army control. Between August 6 and 18, the concentration of the French army required 4,035 trains running on the ten lines organized by the military. Local companies were also affected by the requisition.

A few events disrupted the concentration: the first took place on August 7, when an accident at Brienne blocked the E line (from Toulouse) and traffic was redirected to the D line (from Bordeaux); but on August 8, a second incident on the saturated D line caused delays to the landings of the 12th and 17th corps. On August 10, the train carrying the headquarters of the 55th reserve division was hit at Sompuis at around 5:30 a.m. by one of the 313rd regiment's trains: the collision killed six and injured 25; as for the collision, the officers' wagon was "smashed to pieces", injuring seven, including General Leguay; convoys on the F line were delayed by twenty hours. There were also wagon fires and a number of accidents: for example, on August 6, a soldier from the 61st infantry regiment in [REDACTED] "perched on the brakeman's cab of a wagon hit a structure and was killed outright" before the Givors-Canal station.

As for the French Army of Africa, it provided two divisions from Algeria and Tunisia, as well as a division taken from the Moroccan occupation corpsThe Moroccan occupation corps numbered 82,000 men in 1914, the majority of whom remained in the country. as planned; but these three divisions, made up of regiments of Zouaves, Algerian Tirailleurs, Legionnaires, Spahis and African Chasseurs, were vulnerable during their crossing. On August 4, the Kaiserliche Navy cruisers SMS Goeben and [REDACTED] and Bône, before fleeing as the British ships approached. The French crossing was uneventful after this surprise, with the [REDACTED] Algerian divisions landing in Sète and Marseille, while the Moroccan division ("division de marche d'infanterie coloniale du Maroc") did so in Bordeaux.  Army creation 
alt=Autochrome (color photo) of an airplane.|thumb|Military aeronautics in 1914 was no more than a subdivision of the army, with 216 aircraft grouped into squadrons. There were also a few large airships and tethered balloons. Here, a Caudron G.3.
The transport lines supplied the troops needed to form, from August 5 onwards, the five maneuver armies of Plan XVII, which foresaw a French offensive towards Elsaß-Lothringen (German Alsace-Lorraine) and the possibility of a meeting in the Belgian Ardennes. [REDACTED] armies were thus massed in Lorraine and around Belfort: the 1st Army (commanded by General [REDACTED] and comprising the 7th, 8th, 13th, 14th and 21st Corps) deployed on the slopes of the [REDACTED], relying on the fortified regions of Belfort and Épinal (its mission was to attack to the southeast towards Mulhouse and above all to the northeast towards Sarrebourg); [REDACTED] 9th, 15th, 16th, 18th and 20th corps) deployed on the [REDACTED] plateau, relying on the stronghold of Toul (its mission was to attack to the northeast towards Morhange); the 3rd army (general Ruffey: 4th, 5th and [REDACTED] corps) deployed in Woëvre, relying on the fortified town of Verdun (its more static mission was to guard the German fortifications at [REDACTED]). In the event of a German violation of Belgian neutrality, a strong French left wing guarded the Ardennes massif: [REDACTED] (General Lanrezac: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 10th and 11th Corps) was deployed in the Ardennes department opposite the [REDACTED] gap, with the 4th Army (General [REDACTED]: 12th and 17th Corps, as well as the Colonial Corps) in reserve astride the Argonne and in the Barrois, and the Cavalry Corps in reserve around Mézières.

Only the active divisions were placed in the front line, with the reserve divisions held back until they could be properly taken over and further trained. Four "groups of reserve divisions" were therefore concentrated behind the front line: the first group (58th, 63rd and 66th reserve divisions) around Vesoul (behind the 1st Army), the second group (59th, 68th and [REDACTED] divisions) around Nancy-Toul (at the disposal of the 2nd Army), the third group (54th, 55th and 56th divisions) around Verdun and Saint-Mihiel (at the disposal of the 3rd Army) and the fourth group (51st, 53rd and 69th divisions) around [REDACTED] (behind the 5th Army). The commander-in-chief kept in general reserve the two divisions provided by the 19th corps (37th and 38th, from Algeria), the 44th active division (dispersed in the Alps, facing Italy), the southeastern reservists (the 64th, 65th, 74th and 75th reserve divisions, in the Alps), as well as the divisions assigned to the "mobile defense of [REDACTED]" (57th at Belfort, 71st at Épinal, 72nd at Verdun and 73rd at Toul), while the Minister retained control of the 67th (at the Mailly camp) and the 61st and 62nd reserve divisions (in the entrenched camp of Paris).

The thirteen territorial infantry divisions were the last to be formed, and their concentration continued until August 19. Commanded by General [REDACTED], nine of these divisions were intended for maneuver, hence their name "territorial field divisions": the 91st at Draguignan within the Alps army (in case of an Italian threat); the 84th and 88th assigned to the entrenched camp of Paris (for mobile defense); the 81st and 82nd at [REDACTED] (in case of a German naval landing); the 87th concentrated near Cherbourg (for coastal protection); finally, the 90th and 92nd divisions placed at Perpignan and Bayonne to guard the Spanish border. The last four divisions, the 83rd, 85th, 86th and 89th, were garrisoned in the entrenched camp of Paris, with limited means of transport, hence their name of "territorial site divisions". As Italian and Spanish neutrality was confirmed at the beginning of August, and the [REDACTED] entry into the war secured the coasts, the field divisions were reassigned to the Northeast, with the exception of the 90th, which was sent to North Africa from August 12.

 Consequences 

 Restriction of freedoms 
alt=Cars stopped by an infantry picket (territorials in uniform) on a main road.|left|thumb|Identity checks for travelers leaving Paris by car, August 9.A "state de siège" (state of emergency) was declared on [REDACTED] (two days before receiving the German declaration of war) in all [REDACTED] departments (including Algeria)Décret du 2 août 1914 portant déclaration de mise en état de siège de l'ensemble du territoire (Decree of August 2, 1914 declaring the entire country to be under siege) published in the Journal officiel of August 3, 1914,  in accordance with  and maintained for the duration of the war.Loi du 5 août 1914 relative à l'état de siège (Law of August 5, 1914 relating to the state of siege), published in the Journal officiel of August 6, 1914,  The proclamation of a state of emergency did not comply with the [REDACTED] law on states of emergency: on the one hand, it should have set a limited duration (in months or, at worst, years), after which Parliament should have decided whether or not to renew it; on the other hand, Parliament should have continued to sit, instead of absenting itself, until [REDACTED], immediately after ratifying the state of emergency. 

Mayors and prefects immediately lost their police powers to the military authorities, allowing the army to ban meetings, search homes and bring civilians before military tribunals (with highly simplified procedures and immediate execution of sentences). However, the General Headquarters remained accountable to the executive, which in turn was accountable to Parliament, for the duration of the state of siege - which was not lifted until November 1919, more than a year after the armistice.

German and Austro-Hungarian residents were evacuated from the North-East and from the strongholds; all foreigners were required to have a residence permit.Décret du 2 août [REDACTED] relatif aux mesures à prendre à l'égard des étrangers stationnés en France (Decree of August 2, 1914 on measures to be taken with regard to foreigners stationed in France), published in the Journal officiel of August 3, 1914,  In Paris, exceptional measures were taken: the gates of the fortified city walls were closed and guarded from 6 p.m. until 6 a.m.; by order of the Prefecture of Police on July 29, drinking establishments had to close at 8 p.m. and restaurants at 9 p.m.; dances were forbidden; most gas burners and electric streetlamps were switched off as part of a blackout.

Elections were suspended, as the majority of the electorate, including several deputies,17 deputies are killed in action during their term of office. The first was Pierre Goujon, radical deputy for Ain and reserve sub-lieutenant in the 229th infantry regiment, who was shot in the head at Méhoncourt near Lunéville on August 25, 1914. were in uniform (women and soldiers did not have the right to vote under the Third Republic) and part of the country was occupied. On [REDACTED], the Senate and Chamber of Deputies were called into extraordinary session from the 4th to vote on a series of emergency laws.
alt=Queue of men along a sidewalk.|thumb|Registration of foreign residents prior to their forced evacuation to Brittany, Paris, August 5.

The freedom and secrecy of correspondence no longer existed: military mail, which was systematically late (making any indiscretions unusable), was checked before dispatch, and letters that were pessimistic, defeatist or giving precise information were seized or redacted (lines crossed out) by the postal censorship services. Freedom of the press was affected by censorship: initially, "information other than that communicated by the government or the command on operations, the order of battle, the number of troops (including wounded, killed or prisoners), defense work", etc., were forbidden, as well as "any information or article concerning military or diplomatic operations likely to favor the enemy and exert an unfortunate influence on the spirit of the army and the population",Loi du 5 août 1914 réprimant les indiscrétions de la presse en temps de guerre (Law of August 5, 1914, repressing press indiscretions in wartime), published in the Journal Officiel of August 6, 1914,  and "substantive articles violently attacking the government or army leaders" and those "tending to the cessation or suppression of hostilities."Circulaire du ministre de la Guerre Millerand du 19 septembre 1914. (Circular from War Minister Millerand, September 19, 1914). The press was checked before printing, and articles deemed unpatriotic were banned from publication, sometimes leaving the space for white rectangles.

 Economic difficulties 
From July 31, the French government took a series of economic decisions to accompany its entry into the war. The export of products that could be used for military purposes was prohibited: arms, munitions and explosives, of course, but also livestock, horses, canned goods, meat, flour, hides, fodder, hay, straw, aeroplanes, aerostats, cars, tires, camping gear, lead,[REDACTED] du 31 juillet 1914 portant prohibition de sortie et de réexportation en suite d'entrepôt, de dépôt, de transit, de transbordement et d'admission temporaire de certains produits et objets (Decree of July 31, 1914 prohibiting the exit and re-export from warehouses, deposits, transit, transshipment and temporary admission of certain products and objects), published in the [REDACTED] officiel of August 1, 1914,  etc. The budget allocated to the Ministry of War was increased by a credit of 208 million francs, covering new expenditure on barracks, remounting, clothing, bedding, furnishings, camping, health equipment, armaments and fortifications.Décret du 31 juillet 1914 ouvrant sur l'exercice 1913 un crédit de 208 237 [REDACTED] applicable à des dépenses non renouvelables intéressant la défense nationale (Decree of July 31, 1914 opening a credit of [REDACTED] from the 1913 fiscal year for non-renewable expenses relating to national defense),  To ensure the administration's workload, some civil servants were left on call, and those mobilized were gradually replaced by retired volunteers (later by women and the disabled). Pigeons were kept under surveillance (civilians were forbidden to move or import pigeons).Décret du 2 août 1914 portant interdiction d'importation de pigeons voyageurs étrangers (Decree of August 2, 1914 prohibiting the import of foreign racing pigeons(, published in the Journal officiel of August 3, 1914, Mass mobilization had immediate economic and social consequences: young adult men and horses (around 135,000 horses in August, 600,000 throughout the war, aged between five and fifteen, as well as mules and donkeys) left for the frontiers, completely disrupting the economy and society. Businesses slowed down or closed temporarily. The press greatly reduced its circulation,For example, the daily Le Temps is now printed on only four pages: see the August 3, 1914 edition.  as mobilization deprived it of some of its staff; mail stopped arriving during the mobilization period; civilian telephone service was suspended;Décret interdisant l'usage du language convenu et des langues étrangères pour la rédaction des télégrammes (Decree prohibiting the use of agreed language and foreign languages in telegrams), published in the Journal officiel of August 2, 1914,  every day, an official dispatch arrived in prefectures and sub-prefectures by telegraph from the Ministry of the Interior, before being posted. Passenger rail traffic was almost totally interrupted during the period of concentration, limited to lines not used by the army. In Montbéliard on August 5, all non-mobilized workers aged 16 to 60 were called by the municipality to work on fortifications at Fort Lachaux. Households stocked up on provisions as early as July 1914, fearing supply difficulties, queues formed in front of banks to withdraw savings and exchange them for gold, so much in fact that on the 30th [REDACTED] suspended convertibility, while some inhabitants evacuated Paris to the south as soon as mobilization was announced. Under the law of [REDACTED], a daily allowance of [REDACTED] [REDACTED] centimes per day was paid to poor families whose "provider" was mobilized.Loi du 5 août 1914 tendant à accorder, pendant la durée de la guerre, des allocations aux familles nécessiteuses dont le soutien serait appelé ou rappelé sous les drapeaux (Law of August 5, 1914 to grant, for the duration of the war, allowances to needy families whose provider has been called up or recalled to serve in the armed forces), promulgated in the [REDACTED] officiel of August 6, 1914,  Fearing a shortage of bread, reserve bakers were granted a 45-day deferment of call-up at the request of mayors, and on August 8 bakery production was limited to a [REDACTED] loaf, while brioches, croissants and pastries were banned. On August 13, the government ordered the deferment of rents for the duration of the war.
alt=Three women pulling a plough to till the soil.|thumb|American propaganda image circa 1917: French women working the land.

Some harvesting and haymaking is still to be done (early August), while the grape harvest is still to come (September and October), and industry has to supply clothing, equipment, weapons and ammunition to the army. The mobilization plan left only 50,000 workers in armaments factories (powder works, artillery arsenals and thirty private suppliers), with rare call-up deferrals and partial replacement of mobilized workers by auxiliaries and non-mobilizables; other industrial sectors temporarily ceased operations. To feed the troops in the short term, the military authorities requisitioned flour, livestock and wine. From the end of 1914 onwards, solutions included recalling skilled workers to the rear ("affectés spéciaux", or special assigned), using female workers ("munitionnettes"), children, foreigners (notably Africans and Chinese), prisoners of war and the disabled.

 Beginning of military operations 
alt=Line of infantrymen.|left|thumb|French infantry advancing in line, bayonets drawn, [REDACTED].
The main consequences were military: general mobilization provided the French army with the manpower it needed to wage war against Germany and the other Central Powers. On August 4, covering troops seized the Vosges passes of La Schlucht ([REDACTED] after receiving notification of the declaration of war), Bussang and Oderen. On August 6, the cavalry corps entered Belgium via Bouillon, Bertrix and Paliseul.Message from General Sordet to the Commander-in-Chief, 7:20 a.m., August 6, 1914 cited in  On August 7, the French 7th Corps crossed the border into Germany and began the conquest of Haute-Alsace.Order from Joffre transmitted by telegram to the commander of [REDACTED], at [REDACTED] on August 5, cited in   On August 14, all units of the 1st and 2nd Armies entered Moselle, while the 3rd, 4th and 5th Armies awaited the Germans along the Ardennes section of the Meuse.Special Instruction No. 6 from General Joffre to the commanders of the 3rd, 4th and 5th armies, August 13, 1914, cited in 

thumb|A French squadron in Toulon harbor: the Bouvet seen from another battleship.
For the French navy, the entry of the British into the war meant that it no longer had to fear the German navy. On August 3, 1914, the Franco-British convention of 1913Franco-British technical agreement of February 10, 1913, repeating that of November 1912 and confirmed by the agreement of August 6, 1914 signed in London. Source:  came into force, entrusting the North Sea, the Strait o Dover and the English Channel to the Royal Navy, while the French took charge of the Mediterranean, with the mission of hunting down enemy cruisers and establishing a naval blockade off Austrian ports. Consequently, only a light squadron of six cruisers was stationed at Cherbourg base (under the command of Rear Admiral Rouyer), supplemented by flotillas of torpedo boats and submarines at Dunkirk, Calais and Boulogne, while the "naval army" of 19 battleships was concentrated at Toulon (commanded by Admiral Boué de Lapeyrère), before moving to Valletta in September. As the [REDACTED] fusiliers marins depot was full, and no landings were initially planned, on August 7 these troops, together with detachments from all the ports, formed two regiments grouped together in a fusiliers marins brigade (6,400 men, led by naval and marine officers). This brigade, commanded by Rear Admiral Ronarc'h, was sent to the stronghold of Paris from August 17, before being sent to the front on October 7.

 Later drafts 
alt=Photograph of several cars filled with conscripts leaving the platform.|thumb|Departure of Class 18, 1917. On the wagons: "To Berlin".
French mobilization continued throughout the First World War, with the successive call-up of the Territorial Army Reserve (classes 1892 to 1888) from December 1914 to April 1915 and, above all, the advance of the classes 1914 (from September 1914, instead of October), 1915 (from December 1914), 1916 (in April 1915), 1917 (in January 1916), 1918 (in April 1917) and 1919 (in April 1918).The early call-up of a class is discussed in the Chamber of Deputies every time, for example during the  (for the '17 class), or the  (for the '19 class) These "rookies" first had to complete their training before going into battle; the class of 1919 was only at the front during the last weeks of the war (this was the case for the "last poilus" Fernand Goux and Pierre Picault). Even imprisoned criminals and ex-convicts were drafted into the Battalions of Light Infantry of Africa.

Conscription was gradually applied in the French colonies, but incorporation was uneven, varying according to status: pieds-noirs reservists were mobilized as early as August 1914, and assigned to zouave units; inhabitants of the "old colonies" (Saint Pierre and Miquelon, Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana, the four communes of Senegal, Réunion, the Indies, New Caledonia and Polynesia) provided the manpower for colonial units (mainly colonial infantry regiments); natives (not considered as French citizens, but "subjects") of North Africa, West Africa, Equatorial Africa, Madagascar, the Somali coast, the Comoros and Indochina were more gradually forced into service, a first voluntary service (often encouraged or even forced by local chiefs), completed fairly limited call-ups,Decree dated February 7, 1912, instituting recruitment by call-up of "black natives of the French West Africa group", providing that they "may in all circumstances be designated to continue their service outside the territory of the colony" and specifying that "the duration of active service is four years". Source:  then by mass conscription from 1915From April 1, 1915 for Indochina and after the decree of October 9, 1915 for AOF. Source:  into units of Algerian, Senegalese, Moroccan, Tunisian, Malagasy, Tonkinese, Annamite and Somali tirailleurs. In total, all colonies combined, 583,450 men were gradually drafted,  leading to several uprisings in the colonies.

The first estimate of the total number of men mobilized during the conflict was published in [REDACTED] by MP Louis Marin (who, as budget recorder, needed to know how many families needed to be compensated), based on a report from the Army Staff. According to this document, which has since been widely reprinted, France mobilized a total of 8,410,000 men between August 2, 1914, and January 1, 1919, including 7,935,000 French and 475,000 colonials ([REDACTED] Algerians, 136,000 Senegalese, [REDACTED] Tunisians, 42,500 Indochinese, 34,000 Moroccans, 34,000 [REDACTED] and 3,000 Somalis). Among these, 1,329,640 died as a result of the fighting, to which must be added around three million wounded (including 700,000 disabled).

 Historiography 
Right from the start of [REDACTED], the main subject of historical research was not mobilization itself, but the causes and, above all, the people responsible for the conflict. The first historian to really look into the subject of mobilization was Charles Petit-Dutaillis, medievalist and rector of the Grenoble academy in [REDACTED], who ordered all teachers in the Isère, Drôme and Hautes-Alpes regions to report on the attitude of the local population in the early days. This rector's initiative was passed on to the Minister of Public Instruction, Albert Sarraut, who decided to send out a circular dated [REDACTED], instructing all non-mobilized teachers to keep notes on war-related events, starting with mobilization. During and after the conflict, it was the diplomatic aspects (always linked to the question of responsibilities) and military aspects (essentially operations) that dominated historical production, with the work of [REDACTED] in particular.

The gradual publication of soldiers' testimonies did nothing to change this: for most of the twentieth century, the almost exclusive vision of this entry into the war, printed and taught, was that of general acceptance of the conflict by the population and the departure of the soldiers "avec la fleur au fusil" ,or "[with] the flower on the rifle" (expression used as the title of Jean Galtier-Boissière's testimonial, published in 1928), interpreted as an enthusiastic surge reflecting the spirit of revenge on Germany. The success of this mythical vision of the French entry into the war can be explained by three factors. The first was the immediate usefulness of a mobilization that was presented as enthusiastic, and which was the popular equivalent of the Sacred Union, both of which seemed to emanate from the people as a whole, whereas they were merely the fruit of circumstance. Secondly, the images conveyed by the press and the writings of intellectuals exalting the war contributed powerfully to forging this myth of the flower in the gun. Finally, this representation makes it possible to transfer responsibility for the conflict onto the political leaders, with the crowds letting themselves be carried away by their naivety, without there being any question of their consenting to the war. This consensus was suited to an interwar French population that was both patriotic and pacifist, since it was as compatible with a right-wing opinion (the war was triggered by patriotism and the Germans) as it was with a left-wing opinion (the real perpetrators of the carnage were the politicians and, more generally, the elites).

In the early 1960s, Jean-Jacques Becker made the study of public opinion at the time of the French entry into the war the subject of his thesis, supervised by Renouvin. Since Becker doubted the consensus, he set out to find sources that would show the state of public opinion in [REDACTED], and found Petit-Dutaillis's compilation in the library and archive center La contemporaine. Using schoolteachers' reports, cross-referenced with other sources (press, prefectoral records, etc.), he challenged the myth of "la fleur au fusil." He remained convinced, however, that the French massively embraced the war as a national cause. While [REDACTED] thesis is undisputed for the start of the war, other historians such as Jules Maurin and Philippe Boulanger note that, after the first three months, voluntary enlistments abandoned their patriotic character in favor of a survival strategy. Indeed, being called up early enabled volunteers to choose their brach of assignment. Volunteers were more likely to choose the artillery or navy, reputed to be less deadly than the infantry. This observation therefore undermines the idea that the French always consented to war.

Historian Nicolas Mariot refutes the idea that the war was the "melting pot of a class union, social inequalities of French society in the 1900s persisted under the uniform" by studying the letters and diaries of intellectuals such as Apollinaire and the philosopher Alain, who were either ordinary soldiers or low-ranking soldiers at the front. These intellectuals regretted that their comrades-in-arms from the common people (peasants, craftsmen or workers) did not share their ideals, many of them patriotic. Feeling socially isolated despite an overcrowding that disturbed them, they had little patience for popular swearing or drinking parties. The common soldier looked on them with more suspicion than to the officer, who is often a man designated by rank.

title: Angel Down (novel)
text:
[REDACTED] is a World War I novel with a narrative structure that is a continuously streaming monologue, consisting of one continuous sentence, from the first page of the novel to its last page. The protagonist is a draft dodger and then an army private who encounters an angel on the battlefield. It was written by Daniel Kraus, an [REDACTED] author. It was published by First Atria Books, and imprint of Simon & Schuster, in July 2025.10 Best Books of 2025.The New York Times*

Premise
[REDACTED] [REDACTED] soldiers near the end of World War I, during the Meuse-Argonne offensive, are on a bloody battlefield in France.  Major General Reis, who is focused on his own advancement, orders an infantryman, Private First Class Cyril Bagger to investigate an unearthly shrieking sound that is causing the troops to go insane. [REDACTED] is sent out with four other soldiers, a group of misfits. First there is Arno, who is young and innocent. Next is [REDACTED] who is very much a brute. Then there is Goodspeed who is nervously "squirming," and Veck, who is suffering from severe shell shock.

The five men discover the source of the sound is an angel, and she looks like women that each of the men recognize. She is tangled in barbed wire and emitting an very bright aura. They believe Major General Reis will try to exploit the angel for his own benefit and career advancement. Determined to keep her away from Reis, the soldiers desert their post. They carry the angel, dodging artillery fire while arguing with each other. Each man tries to gain favor with the angel hoping she will grant their personal wishes.

Writing style
According to Publishers Weekly, Kraus builds the tension with the rhythm of his writing, creating a sense of non-stop action because the entire story is a single, continuous sentence. Despite the pacing, the writing is also poetic, as there are lyrical passages like "Bagger sits up with vision aswirl and shoos away the filthy pelt of air, the pigeon-gray smoke and eyeball-white fog." Ben H. Winters of The New York Times says that this novel starts at the outset in the middle of a sentence and in the middle of a battle, while the narrative ends in a comma indicating that there is no conclusion, only continuation.

[REDACTED] also says that the text shows an exemplary example of the "additive style", in which the "writer's prose is associative and spontaneous, piling up new facts and ideas without necessarily spelling out their relationships. The additive style — as distinct from the precise and ordered subordinating style — suggests that the relationship between events, their quote-unquote 'meaning,' is as uncertain in stories as it is in life."

According to Kirkus Reviews, Kraus structured the entire novel as one extended run-on sentence, broken up only by paragraph indentation. This structure works by "giving the story a relentless and intense rhythm."

Themes
Kirkus Reviews says that in the realm of horror, the novel vividly portrays the violence, and blood and guts of the battlefield. This continuous run-on sentence structure is applied to "keep a story moving." According to Kirkus Reviews, the latter part of the book asks philosophical questions about: Why people seem naturally inclined to wage war. What force or idea might be strong enough to stop this cycle of conflict.

Reception
According to Publishers Weekly, the novel is a vigorous and fresh take on the war novel genre. Winters, of The New York Times says, "Angel Down, mysterious and full of grace, may work a similar power on its readers, even as it walks the fields of death."

Awards
In 2025, this received noted kudos from the following media platforms:

 [REDACTED] Top 10 Book Of 2025
 People Magazine Best Books of 2025 
 New York Times Notable Book Of 2025
 Vulture Magazine's Best Books Of 2025

 National Best SellerAngel Down webpage Simon & Schuster. Accessed January 9, 2026.

Film adaptation
In January 2026, a film adaptation was announced to be in development at Imagine Entertainment, who produced a film adaptation of Kraus's previous novel Whalefall.
